name: Magical thinking
statement: Magical thinking is reasoning by contact and by resemblance: juice a sterilised cockroach has touched stays spoiled, and fudge moulded as dog faeces stops being food.
meaning: Three different things travel under this name and they do not share an evidence base. The anthropological sense is Frazer's and Mauss's, two laws abstracted from ritual practice in traditional cultures: contagion, once in contact always in contact, and similarity, the image equals the object. The clinical sense is a symptom dimension, measured by the Magical Ideation Scale and the Thought-Action Fusion Scale, and studied in obsessive-compulsive disorder and the schizophrenia spectrum. The experimental sense is a set of laboratory demonstrations that ordinary educated adults act on both laws when food and disgust are involved. This entry's verdict covers the third. The experimental claim is about behaviour, not doctrine. Rozin and his colleagues argued that people who reject the cockroach juice know it is safe and say so. They reject it anyway. That is why the paper describes the effects as operating at gut level rather than as beliefs anyone would defend.

origin.who: Paul Rozin, Linda Millman and Carol Nemeroff
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Frazer and Mauss named the two laws at the turn of the twentieth century to describe ritual in traditional cultures. The 1986 paper took them into a laboratory room in Philadelphia and tested them on Americans, which is the move that made the idea a psychological finding rather than an ethnographic one.

evidence: Fifty people from the University of Pennsylvania community sat through a single session, 17 men and 33 women, aged 17 to 50 with a mean of 23.6, about half of them students. Each rated items on a 200 mm line anchored at 'dislike extremely' and 'like extremely'. A dried, sterilised cockroach about 4 cm long was dropped into a glass of juice, stirred for five seconds and removed with a new spoon; a plastic birthday candleholder went into the other glass as a control. Ratings of the roached juice fell 102 points against 3 points for the control, a net drop of 98.82 with a standard deviation of 71.62, p < .001, in the predicted direction for 46 of 49 subjects. Fudge moulded into the shape of dog faeces was rated 47.18 points below the same fudge shaped as a disc, and rubber imitation vomit 49.26 points below a rubber sink stopper. Two bottles of sucrose were labelled by the experimenter, one Sucrose and one Sodium Cyanide, with the subject told in advance that both held sugar. Forty-one of 50 preferred to drink from the sucrose bottle, a mean gap of 30.58 points, and only one subject suggested the cyanide bottle might actually hold cyanide. When 38 subjects stuck the labels on themselves the gap fell to 16.5 points, t = 2.60, p < .02. Forty-seven subjects threw darts at photographs: accuracy dropped 11.32 mm for John F. Kennedy and 11.02 mm for the face of the person they liked most, p < .02 in both cases. The paper also reports the measures that did not work. Darts at Hitler and at a disliked person moved 2.11 mm and 4.91 mm, neither reaching significance. A toothbrush used by the person the subject was most attracted to was predicted to gain value and lost it, 19.68 points in the wrong direction, p < .01. Serving fresh juice of the kind that had been roached moved ratings 11.33 points, t = 1.74, p < .05 one-tailed, with only 30 of 49 subjects going the predicted way.

replication.headline: The food-contagion effect reappears in two societies with almost no exposure to germ theory, at rejection rates above 90%, but no preregistered direct replication of the 1986 session was found.
replication.detail: Apicella and colleagues ran contagion scenarios with Hadza hunter-gatherers in Tanzania and Tannese subsistence farmers on Vanuatu. Hyena meat, a cough and arrow poison each briefly entered a pot of honey or of boiling broth and were then removed. Mean rejection across the three contaminants was 94% for both foods, against 68% when the item was a bead from a headband. Six Fisher's exact tests separated contaminants from the bead, all at p < 0.001. On Tanna, 63 participants across three age bands judged eight scenarios involving a pot of yams. Endorsement of eating ran at 0.16 of 4 contaminated items against 0.98 of 4 control items, F(1, 63) = 36.11, p < 0.0001, partial eta-squared 0.367, with no effect of age, F(2, 60) = 2.40, p = 0.099. Hejmadi, Rozin and Siegal put the same task to 125 Hindu Indian and 106 American children. Once the contaminant had been taken out again, 4- to 5-year-olds rejected the juice 64.5% of the time on average and 8-year-olds 89.5%. With the contaminant still present, 59 of 82 Indian 4- to 5-year-olds rejected all three contaminants against 33 of 75 Americans, chi-square(1, N = 157) = 11.93, p < .001. An independent consumer laboratory found the same thing without disgust at full strength. Morales and Fitzsimons gave 95 undergraduates a shopping basket in which feminine napkins either did or did not touch a package of cookies. Quality ratings of the cookies fell from 6.99 to 5.34, F(1, 91) = 20.22, p < .001. Rozin later put the properties to 198 American adults on Prolific in June 2020, asking about the coronavirus. A total of 110, or 56%, said a single virus particle would carry a 50% chance of infection, and 87, or 45%, reported no drop in discomfort when the viruses had sat in a laboratory for a year.

study.cite: Apicella, C. L., Rozin, P., Busch, J. T. A., Watson-Jones, R. E., & Legare, C. H. (2018). Evidence from hunter-gatherer and subsistence agricultural populations for the universality of contagion sensitivity. Evolution and Human Behavior, 39(3), 355-363.

limits: No effect sizes are printed in the structured fields, because nothing measures the same quantity twice. The original reports millimetre shifts on a rating line, the cross-cultural work reports rejection rates, and pairing them would invent a comparison neither paper makes. The verdict covers negative contagion in the food and disgust domain, which is the part of the 1986 paper that later work has gone back to. Positive contagion and the dart-throwing test of similarity were weak or reversed in the original itself and no replication of either was located. Rozin is an author on both the cross-cultural study and the developmental one, so these are extensions by the founding laboratory rather than independent tests; Morales and Fitzsimons is the one independent demonstration used here. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and the Open Science Framework found no preregistered direct replication of Rozin, Millman and Nemeroff. The nearest item is a student project in the Hagen Cumulative Science Project replicating study 3 of Fedotova and Rozin, whose post-data report is not public and is therefore not used. Two arithmetic problems in the sources are worth flagging. Apicella and colleagues print F(1, 63) for an analysis whose other tests carry 60 error degrees of freedom. Hejmadi and colleagues describe 44 of 82 children as 72%, a percentage that belongs to the preceding paragraph, so only their contaminant-present figures are quoted above. Rozin, Markwith and Ross's 1990 follow-up on labels reading 'not sodium cyanide' could not be obtained and is named rather than described.
misreadings: The three senses get quoted as one body of evidence. Eddy's review of 191 studies found the Thought-Action Fusion Scale in 101 of them and the Magical Ideation Scale in 26, and none of that literature measures whether anyone will drink the cockroach juice. A high magical ideation score is a marker on the psychosis spectrum. Chapman and colleagues followed 508 people for ten years. High scorers on that scale had more psychotic disorders and more psychotic-like experiences than 153 controls. It is not a measure of the effects described above, and the two have no shared instrument. The developmental story is told backwards as often as not. Eddy records magical thinking as a normal part of childhood between the ages of 2 and 7 that fades. Nemeroff and Rozin write that contagion is grown into rather than grown out of, absent below age 4 and first appearing at 4 or 5. Both can be true because they are about different things, and a page that treats them as one construct has the arrow pointing the wrong way half the time. Reading the 1986 paper as a finding about superstition also inverts its argument. Its subjects said the juice was safe, could not explain their refusal, and were embarrassed by it. The paper is usually cited as though all fourteen of its measures worked; three did not, and the lover's-toothbrush result came out backwards. Tempting fate, which has its own entry, is a magical-thinking judgement of a narrower kind, and its evidence does not carry over. That effect survives at d = 0.18. A sterilised cockroach costs a glass of juice half the rating scale.

Nemeroff, C., & Rozin, P. (2018). Back in touch with contagion: some essential issues. Journal of the Association for Consumer Research, 3(4), 612-624. The later review by the original authors, and the source for the eight properties of contagion and for the claim that it appears at age 4 or 5.

Eddy, C. M. (2026). The many manifestations of magical thinking: a systematic review. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 17, 1759906. The source for the counts of instruments across 191 studies and for the clinical sense of the term.

Eckblad, M., & Chapman, L. J. (1983). Magical ideation as an indicator of schizotypy. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 51(2), 215-225. The paper the Magical Ideation Scale comes from; the record carries no abstract and the article itself was not obtained.

Bibliographic record verified at Crossref; the article was not obtained and nothing is quoted from it.
